modelIdentification.name: Restaurant FOM Module Example
modelIdentification.purpose: To define an HLA object model for a restaurant federation
modelIdentification.description: This object model is intended to define the HLA Federation Object Model for a restaurant simulation. It is a standalone FOM module since it depends on no other FOM module other than the standard HLA MIM module.
modelIdentification.useLimitation: Derived models must reference this document
modelIdentification.useHistory: Originally used as an example in the DoD HLA 1.3 specification
Used as an example in the HLA IEEE1516.2-2000 specification
Used as an example in the HLA IEEE1516.2-2010 specification after conversion to a FOM module (MIM information stripped out)
Used as an example in the HLA IEEE 1516.2-2025 specification after conversion to a FOM module
modelIdentification.other: See Mobil International Restaurant Guide for more information

note.label: Note2
note.semantics: For most general-purpose restaurant simulations, this will be Subscribe only.

note.label: Note3
note.semantics: Merit raises are not provided according to any regular time interval; they are provided on a supervisor’s recommendation based on evidence of exceptional effort and performance.

note.label: Note4
note.semantics: Years of service are a factor in any merit raise. This value is only changed on the anniversary of the employee’s hire.

note.label: Note5
note.semantics: Sometimes a dish can be modified to be gluten- or wheat-free, e.g. gluten-free pasta can be used for some pasta dishes, but dishes like ravioli and lasagna are usually pre-made with wheat pasta and can’t be modified.

note.label: Note6
Note7
note.semantics: Gluten is found in three grains: wheat, barley, and rye. Gluten intolerant individuals will have varying degrees of negative, but not necessarily debilitating, reactions to these foods. Individuals with Celiac disease will have debilitating reactions to these foods and suffer long-term, potentially life-threatening effects. Those with wheat allergies may suffer immediate, life-threatening reactions, but may be able to eat barley and rye. Depending on levels of sensitivity, cross-contamination in the kitchen can be dangerous to the extent that separate food preparation areas and tools are required.
